argument.title: Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood

atoms.A: God lacks proper parts (the claim taken as the most plausible understanding of divine simplicity)
atoms.C: The symmetry formulation of divine simplicity holds
atoms.D: Instantiation can be modelled as parthood (objects as fusions of their properties)
atoms.E: God and omniscience are mutual parts with respect to similarity while remaining numerically distinct
atoms.F: Proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric similarity-based parthood
atoms.G: Divine simplicity can viably be formulated as the thesis that God is part of all God's parts
atoms.H: Proper parthood is irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive

argument.missing_premise: Proper parthood is non-symmetric parthood, and the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is the thesis that God is part of all God's parts. [B & (C -> G)]

W7212186029.c001.text: Under classical mereology, something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.
W7212186029.c001.quote: Under classical mereology, the two formulations of DDS are equivalent – something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.

W7212186029.c002.text: On plausible non-antisymmetric mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being part of all its parts without being identical to them.
W7212186029.c002.quote: On some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts, even if it is not identical to all its parts.

W7212186029.c003.text: Divine simplicity can be formulated as God being an improper part of all of God's improper parts.
W7212186029.c003.quote: Thus, it is possible to formulate DDS as a thesis saying that God is simple in the sense of being a part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation of DDS.

W7212186029.c004.text: The symmetry formulation is a viable understanding of divine simplicity, particularly concerning God's relation to God's attributes.
W7212186029.c004.quote: this paper will argue that the symmetry formulation is a viable way of understanding DDS, particularly as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes.

W7212186029.c005.text: Divine simplicity cannot plausibly mean that God lacks improper parts, because reflexivity makes God an improper part of Godself.
W7212186029.c005.quote: DDS cannot plausibly be interpreted as a thesis that God lacks parts in this sense, because the reflexivity of improper parthood implies that God has at least himself as a part.

W7212186029.c006.text: Divine simplicity is most plausibly understood as the claim that God lacks proper parts.
W7212186029.c006.quote: Instead, DDS is more plausibly understood as saying that God lacks proper parts – call this the mereological formulation of DDS.

W7212186029.c007.text: If proper parthood is distinct parthood, the claim that God has no proper parts is equivalent to the identity formulation of divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c007.quote: If proper parthood is distinct parthood, the mereological formulation of DDS is equivalent to the common understanding of DDS as a thesis identifying God with his parts – call this the identity formulation of DDS.

W7212186029.c008.text: If proper parthood is non-symmetric parthood, the claim that God has no proper parts yields the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c008.quote: But if proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood, then explicating proper parthood in the mereological formulation yields the symmetry formulation of DDS.

W7212186029.c009.text: Without antisymmetry, the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is strictly weaker than the identity formulation.
W7212186029.c009.quote: Accordingly, DDS under the symmetric formulation is strictly weaker than under the identity formulation: if God lacks distinct parts, he also lacks non-symmetric parts, but not vice versa.

W7212186029.c010.text: The symmetry formulation is a viable and distinct formal mereological understanding of divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c010.quote: The upshot is that as far as the formal mereological framework goes, the symmetry formulation presents a viable and distinct way of understanding DDS.

W7212186029.c011.text: The symmetry formulation is viable if parthood is antisymmetric or proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric, and distinct from identity when parthood is non-antisymmetric.
W7212186029.c011.quote: The viability of the symmetry formulation is given by the fact that it is equivalent to the mereological formulation if parthood is assumed antisymmetric, or if proper parthood is defined as nonsymmetric parthood, either of which would be independently plausible. The distinctness of the symmetry formulation from the identity formulation is given by the fact that the two are non-equivalent whenever parthood is not antisymmetric, which is also a reasonable possibility.

W7212186029.c012.text: Divine simplicity concerning attributes distinguishes God from other entities more clearly than simplicity concerning other forms of parthood.
W7212186029.c012.quote: One reason for this focus is that simplicity with respect to attributes would set God apart from other entities more distinctly than simplicity with respect to other kinds of parthood, in line with a common motivation for DDS from God’s transcendence.

W7212186029.c013.text: Instantiation can be modelled as parthood because objects may be understood as mereological fusions of their properties.
W7212186029.c013.quote: On the mereological bundle theory suggested by Laurie Paul (2002, 2006, 2012, 2017), for instance, objects are mereological fusions of the properties they bear.

W7212186029.c014.text: When objects are collections of their properties, an object's instantiating a property makes that property a part of the object with respect to similarity.
W7212186029.c014.quote: Whenever an object o has a property p, whatever bears a property more similar to p also thereby becomes more similar to o; hence p is part of o with respect to similarity.

W7212186029.c015.text: Objects can, in principle, be parts of properties with respect to similarity.
W7212186029.c015.quote: It is also possible, at least in principle, for objects to be part of properties with respect to similarity.

W7212186029.c016.text: God and omniscience can be mutual parts with respect to similarity while remaining numerically distinct.
W7212186029.c016.quote: it is also possible, at least in principle, for this symmetric parthood relation to hold while God remains numerically distinct from his omniscience.

W7212186029.c017.text: Similarity-based parthood is not generally antisymmetric if distinct things can be mutual parts.
W7212186029.c017.quote: The possibility of such cases would imply that parthood with respect to similarity is not generally antisymmetric.

W7212186029.c018.text: Defining proper parthood as non-symmetric similarity-based parthood makes proper parthood irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.
W7212186029.c018.quote: If proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood with respect to similarity, it would immediately be irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.

W7212186029.c019.text: Relations between objects and properties can be modelled mereologically so that the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is viable for God and attributes.
W7212186029.c019.quote: The upshot is that the relations between objects and their properties can be modelled mereologically in such a way that DDS on the symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about the relation between God and his attributes.

W7212186029.c020.text: Metaphysical dependence is more plausibly entailed by proper parthood than by improper parthood.
W7212186029.c020.quote: Instead, the parthood-dependence relation is more plausibly understood as an entailment from proper parthood (in some sense) to dependence.

W7212186029.c021.text: Dependence should follow from non-symmetric parthood rather than from distinct parthood generally because dependence is usually asymmetric.
W7212186029.c021.quote: it would square better with our usual understanding for dependence to follow from non-symmetric parthood, rather than distinct parthood more generally.

W7212186029.c022.text: If dependence tracks non-symmetric parthood, aseity requires only that God lack non-symmetric parts.
W7212186029.c022.quote: And if dependence tracks non-symmetric parthood, then the doctrine of aseity requires only that God lack non-symmetric parts, as the symmetry formulation posits.

W7212186029.c023.text: The symmetry formulation preserves the transcendence motivation for divine simplicity because ordinary objects are not parts of their properties.
W7212186029.c023.quote: The symmetry formulation maintains this motivation, because ordinary objects are not parts of their properties.

W7212186029.c024.text: The symmetry formulation of divine simplicity makes God unique by holding that God and all divine attributes are mutual parts.
W7212186029.c024.quote: Hence, the symmetry formulation makes God unique by positing that God is part of all his attributes, which are also all parts of each other.

W7212186029.c025.text: Necessary parthood relations between God and the attributes constituting God's intrinsic nature entail that God has those attributes necessarily and unchangingly.
W7212186029.c025.quote: And if God is taken to bear mutual and necessary parthood relations to the properties that constitute his intrinsic nature, God would have these properties necessarily and hence unchangingly, which yields immutability.

W7212186029.c026.text: Things that are mutual parts have the same parts and wholes, and are therefore mereologically indiscernible.
W7212186029.c026.quote: the transitivity of parthood implies that whenever two things are parts of each other, they have all the same parts and are parts of all the same things.

W7212186029.c027.text: The symmetry formulation allows God's nature to lack discernible divisions even if divine attributes are not numerically identical.
W7212186029.c027.quote: Hence, under the symmetry formulation of DDS, God’s nature can be said to admit no discernible divisions, even if his attributes are not numerically identical to each other.

W7212186029.c028.text: The symmetric formulation retains the common motivations for divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c028.quote: the discussion above shows that the symmetric formulation retains the motivations of DDS.

W7212186029.c029.text: If God is identical with omniscience, God is a property or property instance, which may be self-exemplifying and causally inert.
W7212186029.c029.quote: First, if God is his omniscience, then God is a property (or property instance). Besides being unintuitive, this might imply that God’s omniscience is self-exemplifying, and make it difficult to explain how God can interact with the world if properties (or property instances) are causally inert.

W7212186029.c030.text: If God is both omniscience and omnipotence, identity's transitivity implies that omniscience and omnipotence are identical despite appearing distinct.
W7212186029.c030.quote: Second, if God is simultaneously his omniscience and his omnipotence, the transitivity of identity seems to imply that God’s omniscience is his omnipotence; but the two seem intuitively to be distinct.

W7212186029.c031.text: If resemblance consists in shared properties, divine simplicity implies that anyone good like God possesses all God's attributes and perhaps God himself.
W7212186029.c031.quote: if resemblance is understood as property sharing, then DDS seems to imply that someone who resembles God by being good also possesses all of God’s attributes, and perhaps even God himself.

W7212186029.c032.text: The symmetry formulation can address all three difficulties concerning God's distinction from divine attributes.
W7212186029.c032.quote: This section will argue that the symmetry formulation can address all three difficulties.

W7212186029.c033.text: Because God and divine attributes can be numerically distinct under the symmetry formulation, it does not entail that God is a property or that divine attributes are identical.
W7212186029.c033.quote: DDS under the symmetry formulation allows for God and his attributes to be numerically distinct from each other, and hence does not entail that God is a property (instance), or that God’s attributes are all identical.

W7212186029.c034.text: Resemblance can consist in possessing sufficiently similar properties rather than sharing a property, preventing goodness-based resemblance from giving creatures God and all divine attributes as parts.
W7212186029.c034.quote: Then, for someone to resemble God in terms of goodness requires not that they have God’s goodness itself, but only that they have a sufficiently similar property like (say) the property of imperfect goodness.

W7212186029.c035.text: If God necessarily exists and is identical with every divine aspect, divine acts and knowledge become necessary, eliminating free will and contingent truths.
W7212186029.c035.quote: But if all of God’s acts are necessary, then God cannot act differently from how he actually does, which implies that God lacks free will. Moreover, God’s omniscience entails that for any true proposition p, God knows that p.

W7212186029.c036.text: Divine simplicity can allow contingent mutual parthood relations between God and some attributes, while requiring necessity only for attributes constituting God's intrinsic nature.
W7212186029.c036.quote: The account of God’s immutability suggested in section ‘Motivations’ stipulates that some parthood relations between God and his attributes are necessary, but it does not require that this be the case for all of God’s attributes, only those that constitute his intrinsic nature.

W7212186029.c037.text: If God's willingness to create is not intrinsic, contingent parthood with that willingness permits a possible world where necessary God does not create, making God's actual creative act free.
W7212186029.c037.quote: Then, there is a possible world in which God exists (by necessity), but does not have a willingness to create and hence does not, which implies that God’s actual creative act is free.

W7212186029.c038.text: If God’s willingness to create is temporally necessary but metaphysically contingent, God’s actual creative act remains free.
W7212186029.c038.quote: God’s actual creative act hence remains free in this case.

W7212186029.c039.text: God’s omniscience entails God’s knowledge that snow is white in actuality.
W7212186029.c039.quote: Similarly, in actuality, God knows as an implication of omniscience that snow is white

W7212186029.c040.text: God, God’s omniscience, and God’s knowledge that snow is white are mutually parts of each other.
W7212186029.c040.quote: such that God, his omniscience, and his knowledge that snow is white are all parts of each other.

W7212186029.c041.text: God’s parthood relation with omniscience can be necessary, whereas relations involving God’s knowledge that snow is white can be metaphysically contingent.
W7212186029.c041.quote: The parthood relations between God and his omniscience can be taken to be necessary (since omniscience is in God’s intrinsic nature), while those involving God’s knowledge that snow is white are taken to be (metaphysically) contingent.

W7212186029.c042.text: God could lack knowledge that snow is white while remaining omniscient if snow were not white.
W7212186029.c042.quote: Then, there could be a possible world in which God does not have the knowledge that snow is white, but God remains omniscient because snow is not white.

W7212186029.c043.text: That snow is white is contingently true in actuality.
W7212186029.c043.quote: That snow is white is thus a contingent truth in actuality.

W7212186029.c044.text: Divine simplicity can viably be formulated as the thesis that God is part of all God’s parts.
W7212186029.c044.quote: this paper has argued that there is a viable alternative formulation of DDS as a thesis that God is part of all his parts.

W7212186029.c045.text: Plausible mereological theories treat mereological simplicity as lacking non-symmetric parts, and object–property relations can plausibly be understood as parthood.
W7212186029.c045.quote: The viability of this formulation is suggested by the observations that there are plausible mereological theories under which mereological simplicity consists in lacking non-symmetric parts, and that the relation between objects and their properties can plausibly be understood in terms of parthood.

W7212186029.c046.text: The symmetric formulation of divine simplicity preserves the doctrine’s usual motivations and addresses its usual difficulties.
W7212186029.c046.quote: Moreover, this formulation of DDS retains the doctrine’s usual motivations and addresses its usual difficulties.

W7212186029.c047.text: Under perdurantism, the usual formulation of divine simplicity makes it difficult to explain how God interacts with the world.
W7212186029.c047.quote: But DDS on the usual understanding implies that God has no temporal proper parts, and hence cannot exist across extended periods of time, which makes it difficult to explain how God can interact with the world.

W7212186029.c048.text: The symmetric formulation can reconcile divine simplicity with perdurantism by allowing distinct temporal parts of God if God is part of each of them.
W7212186029.c048.quote: The symmetry formulation offers a possible way of reconciling DDS with perdurantism, since it allows that God can have distinct temporal parts, so long as he is a part (in some plausible sense) of all of them.

W7212186029.c049.text: Whether the symmetric formulation provides a viable divine-simplicity model of God’s relation to time requires further investigation.
W7212186029.c049.quote: Whether this is indeed a viable model of God’s relation to time under DDS requires more thorough investigation in future work

W7212186029.c050.text: Some authors argue that dependence could be symmetric.
W7212186029.c050.quote: Some authors have argued that dependence could be symmetric – see Schaffer (2012), Bliss (2014), Rodriguez-Pereyra (2015), Thompson (2016), Cotnoir (2017), and Barnes (2018).

W7212186029.c051.text: For God's nature, the possibility of symmetric parthood implies that dependence is not generally asymmetric.
W7212186029.c051.quote: Cotnoir (2017) in particular suggests that when it comes to God’s nature, the possibility of symmetric parthood implies that dependence is not generally asymmetric.

W7212186029.c052.text: Some authors have argued that dependence could be symmetric.
W7212186029.c052.quote: Some authors have argued that dependence could be symmetric

W7212186029.c053.text: The possibility of symmetric parthood in God’s nature implies that dependence is not generally asymmetric.
W7212186029.c053.quote: Cotnoir (2017) in particular suggests that when it comes to God’s nature, the possibility of symmetric parthood implies that dependence is not generally asymmetric.

W7212186029.c054.quote: Some authors have argued that dependence could be symmetric

W7212186029.arg1.mp.text: Proper parthood is non-symmetric parthood, and the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is the thesis that God is part of all God's parts.

W7212186029.a1.text: The formulations that God lacks proper parts and that God is identical with all parts are not generally equivalent.
W7212186029.a1.quote: The two formulations are not generally equivalent – on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its (possibly distinct) parts.

W7212186029.a2.text: Divine simplicity can instead be formulated as God being part of all divine parts.
W7212186029.a2.quote: Thus, the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation.

W7212186029.a3.text: The symmetry formulation is viable, retains standard motivations, and addresses objections concerning attribute distinctness and modal collapse.
W7212186029.a3.quote: The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

W7212186029.arg1.r1.text: Proper parthood, as used in the divine simplicity claim, is the similarity-relative relation of c018, and that relation tracks metaphysical constituency closely enough that having no proper parts under it expresses the traditional denial of composition.

W7212186029.arg1.r2.text: Instantiation of God's timelessly and essentially held properties, such as omniscience, can be modelled as parthood because God may be understood as the mereological fusion of those properties, with no claim that this holds for contingent, time-varying properties of ordinary objects.

W7212186029.arg1.r3.text: For God and each of God's parts, parthood is bivalent, so that God's being part of each such part is settled true rather than merely not false.

W7212186029.arg1.r4.text: For God’s essential attributes, similarity-based parthood is restricted to resemblance relations grounded in metaphysical constituency, so merely qualitative similarity between independently constituted things never suffices for parthood.

objections.text: Take a lamp, L, that is switched on at noon and off at one. Its property of being lit is instantiated at noon and not at one. Model instantiation as parthood: L is the fusion of its properties, so 'being lit' is a part of L. Now the lamp is switched off at one, and nothing in L's identity changes, yet the fusion has lost a part. But the fusion of its properties is supposed to be fixed by which properties it has, so the lamp at one o'clock is a different fusion from the lamp at noon, though it is the same lamp. Worse, the lamp also has the property of being a lamp, and that property is shared with every other lamp. A fusion of properties would then overlap with the fusion of a neighbouring lamp, so distinct objects share parts they should not share. Parthood cannot carry instantiation without either losing the lamp's persistence or making distinct objects overlap.
objections.premise_fails_because: c013 fails because treating instantiation as parthood over fusions of properties cannot preserve an object's identity through change in its properties while keeping distinct objects mereologically disjoint, since shared universals and temporary properties break the fusion model.

objections.text: Take a museum that holds two bronze casts, A and B, poured from one mold on the same day. They match atom-for-atom in shape, alloy and patina. On any similarity-based reading of parthood, each counts as part of the other, since everything A is like, B is like too. Yet a conservator melts A down and B stays on its plinth untouched. Nothing of B went into the crucible, so mutual similarity-parthood between distinct things is just duplication, not containment. Now apply this to God and omniscience. For the two to be similarity-parts of each other in both directions, omniscience would have to match God in every respect God has. But God knows that the casts exist, acts, and is omnipotent. Omniscience knows nothing, does nothing, and is not omnipotent. The resemblance holds only one way. Read narrowly, as similarity in the respect of knowing, the case collapses into the casts: mere matching between distinct items. Read broadly, it fails for lack of resemblance.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c016 fails because mutual similarity between numerically distinct items is mere duplication, as with the casts, and God and omniscience don't even match in every respect, so they cannot be genuine mutual parts while staying distinct.

objections.text: A believer describes God as wholly present in every act of understanding, loving, and creating, without treating these as separable components. When Mara prays for wisdom, she believes God knows her question, wills her good, and acts in one indivisible divine reality. She denies that knowledge, will, and action are proper parts of God: none can be detached, counted, or exist independently. Yet she also denies that divine simplicity is merely the absence of proper parts. For her, simplicity additionally means that God’s knowing, willing, and acting are identical with God, rather than distinct features somehow fused into a partless whole. A perfectly partless divine point containing three genuinely distinct, non-identical features would lack proper parts but would not satisfy her understanding of simplicity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c006 fails because lacking proper parts does not by itself entail that God’s attributes are identical with God.

objections.text: A theologian maintains a three-valued parthood catalogue. It records omniscience as part of God, while whether God is part of omniscience is explicitly undetermined. A proper part is defined as a part whose reverse parthood is false, not merely unconfirmed. Omniscience is therefore not a proper part of God, and the catalogue contains no other candidate parts, so “God has no proper parts” is true. Yet “God is part of all God’s parts” is not true, because God’s parthood of omniscience remains undetermined. The absence of asymmetric parthood does not establish reciprocal parthood when undetermined relations are permitted. Premise W7212186029.c008 fails because having no proper parts does not yield symmetry when reverse parthood can be neither true nor false.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7212186029.c008 fails because having no proper parts does not yield symmetry when reverse parthood can be neither true nor false.

objections.text: Consider a lab mereologist, Ada, who holds that God is simple and that God's omniscience and God's power are both parts of God in the similarity sense of c016. Ada accepts that proper parthood is non-symmetric parthood, as the premise says. She then takes the symmetry formulation, God is part of all God's parts, to follow. Now test it. Let Bo be a rival who models proper parthood as strict inclusion of properties. On Bo's model, God's omniscience is a proper part of God only if God is not identical to it, and God is part of omniscience only if omniscience includes God's whole nature. Bo's model makes God part of all God's parts only if each part includes the whole, which is exactly what fails for distinct properties with different modal profiles. Ada's premise assumes that non-symmetric parthood alone yields the symmetry thesis. It does not. Non-symmetric parthood permits a part to fail to contain its whole, so the thesis that God is part of each of God's parts is an extra commitment about the direction of inclusion that the premise leaves unstated.
objections.premise_fails_because: Non-symmetry of proper parthood does not entail that God is part of every God-part, since asymmetry only rules out mutual proper parthood and says nothing about whether each part contains the whole.

objections.text: Consider a chemist, Mara, studying a copper wire. She believes physical objects are composed of their physical constituents: atoms, fields, and their arrangements. She heats the wire, and it loses its coiled shape while every atom stays put. If the wire were a fusion of its properties, losing the property 'coiled' would mean losing a part. But nothing material left the wire. The wire also gains the property 'being thought of by Mara' when she reflects on it, yet no part arrives. The wire's real composition, the things that would show up in any physical inventory, is constant through both changes. Its properties track how its parts are arranged and related. They are not further ingredients. Treating instantiation as parthood confuses what an object is made of with what is true of it. The God case depends on this confusion: omniscience can be a 'part' of God only if parthood has been redefined until it no longer tracks composition. At that point, 'having no proper parts' says nothing about what God is made of.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c013 fails because objects are composed of physical constituents rather than fusions of their properties, so modelling instantiation as parthood confuses predication with composition and leaves the simplicity thesis about something other than real parts.

objections.text: skeptical theism: Mara believes God created a world whose deepest metaphysical structure exceeds human conceptual reach. She observes that a red apple instantiates redness and roundness, but she also believes God may ground these features through divine creative acts rather than by composing the apple from property-parts. When Mara tries to model instantiation as fusion, the model treats properties as separable constituents and assumes that creaturely mereology applies to every metaphysical dependence relation. Yet her own theism supplies reason to deny that assumption: God may create indivisible substances with derivative, intelligible features without those features being parts. Human success in describing ordinary material fusions gives no entitlement to infer that instantiation itself is parthood, especially where the inference is used to characterize God.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c013 fails because finite human mereological models do not license treating every instance-property relation, much less divine reality, as parthood.

objections.text: Consider Ada and Ben, two sculptors who each carve a statue from the same block. Ada's statue is a bronze cast of a horse; Ben's is a marble carving of the same horse shape. Under the similarity-relative relation of c018, Ada's statue and Ben's statue are maximally similar in shape, so each counts as a 'part' of the other on that relation, and neither has a proper part that is not similar to it. Yet the statues share no constituents at all: the bronze and the marble are wholly distinct stuffs, and nothing material of one composes or underlies the other. Parthood-by-similarity therefore holds between things with no metaphysical constituency relation, so the relation does not track constituency. Having no proper parts under this relation would then be compatible with Ada's statue being composed of bronze-matter and form, which is exactly the composition the traditional denial of composition rejects. The inference from 'no proper parts in the similarity sense' to 'no composition' is therefore unlicensed.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise that the similarity-relative relation tracks metaphysical constituency fails, since Ada's bronze horse and Ben's marble horse stand in the similarity-based parthood relation while sharing no constituents, so having no proper parts under that relation does not express denial of composition.

objections.text: In a world with God, God eternally knows that Lina freely chooses tea at noon tomorrow. God’s omniscience is essential and timeless: God cannot cease to know this truth. Yet Lina’s choice remains genuinely free; until noon, she could choose coffee instead. When Lina chooses coffee, the proposition God knows is instead that Lina chooses coffee. God has not gained, lost, or changed any essential property: God eternally knows every truth, whichever free truth obtains. But omniscience is not a property that can be fused with God as a constituent part, because its particular truth-content depends on Lina’s distinct act. Treating omniscience as a mereological part would make a part of God differ with Lina’s choice, contrary to the premise’s claim that the relevant properties are timelessly and essentially held.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.arg1.r2 fails because even essential omniscience can have truth-content dependent on a contingent creaturely act and so cannot be straightforwardly modelled as a timeless constituent part of God.

objections.text: Consider a lab of similarity-based mereology in which parthood is graded. Ada is a cellist whose playing is partly similar to Bo's score-reading, and the lab's stipulated similarity measure assigns Ada's relation to Bo's reading a value of 0.5. The lab's model defines 'part' as holding to a degree, and the relation is only 'settled' when the degree reaches 1 or 0. Now apply this to God and a divine attribute, goodness. Nothing grounds their qualitative match in any shared constituent: they are made of distinct lumps of metal with no common part. Yet the revised premise says similarity grounded in metaphysical constituency is required for parthood, and that merely qualitative similarity between independently constituted things never suffices. Suppose a sculptor now proposes that Ana and Ben be treated as mutual parts with respect to shape, so that the fusion of their shapes is a single shape-bearer. The restriction blocks this only by fiat: it does not say what 'metaphysical constituency' contributes beyond the similarity itself, so the restriction is either idle or it smuggles in a constituency relation that the divine case, where God and God's attributes are not independently constituted, would need to supply by stipulation. rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the wire case shows properties and physical composition come apart, and the argument should not say otherwise. But c013 does not assert that a coiled shape is a physical part of the wire. It asserts a model: the object is treated as a fusion of its properties, and parthood is the similarity-relative relation that the model uses. Mara's point therefore targets the wrong thing unless the model is meant to report composition. The argument's own use of parthood is explicitly relativised: c016 and c015 say mutual parthood holds 'with respect to similarity' and that objects can be parts of properties in that sense, while c018 fixes the formal profile (irreflexive, asymmetric, transitive) of the proper-parthood notion. Once the relation is taken as similarity-based, 'having no proper parts' is a claim about the structure of that relation over God and God's attributes, not a claim about physical inventory. Your strongest rejoinder is that a relation so redefined is no longer parthood, and that the symmetry formulation thereby trades on an equivocation. That is a fair charge against the label, and it is where the argument is weakest. It can be met by accepting that the formulation is a formal reconstruction of simplicity rather than an account of what God is made of, and that the traditional doctrine was itself meant as a denial of metaphysical composition. The modelling claim survives, but only as a claim about formal structure, which the conclusion c044 must be read as expressing.
rounds.revised_premise: Instantiation is modelled as a similarity-relative parthood relation whose formal profile is fixed by the definition of proper parthood; the model is a claim about formal structure, not about physical composition.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You concede the label, but the concession costs more than you allow. The premise c006 is plausible only because "parts" there means metaphysical constituents, which is what the tradition denied. If c044 is merely a formal reconstruction, it no longer formulates *that* doctrine. It formulates a different thesis about a similarity relation, and "viably" becomes unearned. The argument then equivocates between c006 and c044, and your retreat makes the gap explicit rather than closing it.

The wire case also returns inside your model. If instantiation is parthood, God's relational properties, such as *being thought of by Mara*, are parts of God. Is God part of them "with respect to similarity"? If so, similarity-based parthood is so permissive that symmetry with God is cheap and the thesis is trivial. If not, God has contingent proper parts, and simplicity fails on your own terms. Which is it?

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
The wire case does not touch c013 as written. c013 offers a model in which an object is a fusion of its properties and parthood is the similarity-relative relation (c016, c015), not a claim that coiledness is a physical piece of the wire. Mara's inventory is therefore beside the point unless the model is read as reporting composition, which the argument does not do.

Your dilemma about God's relational properties is the sharper challenge. I take the first horn only in a restricted form: God's being part of an attribute holds with respect to similarity, and similarity-based symmetry is not cheap because c018 fixes the relation's formal profile, which excludes trivial symmetry for distinct relata. Relational properties like being thought of by Mara are not thereby parts of God in the composition sense; they are relata whose similarity to God must be assessed, and the model does not guarantee that God is similar to each of them in the required way. So the second horn does not follow automatically: God is not forced to have contingent proper parts, because the model counts only the relevant similarity-parts.

I concede the core of your rejoinder. The traditional doctrine denied metaphysical composition [W7212186029.c006 is plausible only under that reading], and c044 formulates a thesis about a similarity relation, not that doctrine. The equivocation between c006 and c044 is real, and the argument needs a bridging premise it does not supply: that the similarity-relative relation captures the constituent notion of proper parthood that c006 invokes.

Revised premise: Proper parthood, as used in the divine simplicity claim, is the similarity-relative relation of c018, and that relation tracks metaphysical constituency closely enough that having no proper parts under it expresses the traditional denial of composition.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your wire case is a strong objection to treating property-parthood as ordinary material composition. But the argument need not do that. It proposes a distinct, similarity-based mereological relation: when an object is understood as a collection of properties, instantiating a property makes it a part of that object in that respect [W7212186029.c014]. Thus loss of coiledness and acquisition of being thought of by Mara need not involve material departure or arrival; they are changes in similarity-based structure, while the physical inventory remains constant.

That distinction matters in the God case. The intended claim is not that omniscience is a spatial or material ingredient of God, nor that divine simplicity is a thesis about physical inventory. It is that, on a non-antisymmetric parthood theory, God and an attribute may be mutual parts without numerical identity, and so God can lack non-symmetric proper parts by being part of every part [W7212186029.c002; W7212186029.c018].

Still, you correctly expose that c013 is too broad if read as a claim about all ordinary objects or all properties. The argument survives only with a restricted modelling claim: the relevant property-fusion account must apply to divine attributes, and the resulting parthood must be explicitly non-compositional.

Revised premise: For divine attributes, instantiation may be modelled by a non-compositional, similarity-based parthood relation, without implying that attributes are material constituents of God.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c013, read as an unrestricted claim, cannot survive the lamp case. A fusion fixed by the properties an object has at a time will change when the lamp goes off, so the lamp-at-noon and lamp-at-one come out as distinct fusions. The overlap worry also bites: 'being a lamp' is a shared part of every lamp-fusion. I accept both costs for the general model. But the argument's use of c013 concerns God, whose relevant properties, such as omniscience, are timeless and essential. The persistence problem does not arise without temporal variation in the instantiated properties. The overlap cost is one the argument already accepts in c016 and c017, where distinct things are mutual parts with respect to similarity, so it is not a new burden. What the argument cannot keep is the unrestricted wording of c013. Because c013 as written is too broad, I concede that the argument as stated does not survive. It survives with the restricted premise below, which the objection leaves untouched.

Revised premise: Instantiation of God's timelessly and essentially held properties, such as omniscience, can be modelled as parthood because God may be understood as the mereological fusion of those properties, with no claim that this holds for contingent, time-varying properties of ordinary objects.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your temporal case exposes a real underspecification, but not yet a contradiction. The proposal is that, when objects are collections of properties, instantiation makes the relevant property part of the object with respect to similarity [W7212186029.c014]; it is not committed to saying that a persisting lamp is identical at every time to one fixed fusion of timeless universals. A defensible version can take the relevant relata to be time-indexed property instances: being-lit-at-noon is then a similarity-part of L at noon, while its absence at one does not force L’s numerical replacement. Likewise, sharing the repeatable property being-a-lamp does not itself entail an unacceptable result: distinct fusions may overlap without being identical, and the paper’s central framework expressly permits non-antisymmetric parthood where distinct things can be mutual parts [W7212186029.c017]. What matters for the divine-simplicity application is that object–property relations can plausibly be understood as parthood, not that ordinary-object fusions are disjoint or temporally immutable [W7212186029.c045]. Still, you are right that c013, as stated, needs a restriction: without one, its talk of “the fusion of its properties” invites precisely the persistence problem you identify.

Revised premise: Instantiation can be modelled as similarity-based parthood when an object is associated with its time-indexed property instances, so changes in instantiated properties need not entail a change in the object’s numerical identity.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the inference in c008 is not valid under your three-valued catalogue. The argument needs 'no proper parts' to exclude every part of God whose reverse parthood is not established, but your definition excludes only parts whose reverse parthood is false. A part of God for which God's parthood is undetermined survives both your definition and the claim 'God has no proper parts', yet it violates the symmetry formulation. The step from asymmetry to symmetry works only if, for every part of God, reverse parthood is settled as true, which is what the argument's appeal to c018's irreflexive, asymmetric relation implicitly assumed. Your counterexample therefore shows c008 needs a bivalence premise. I see no way to recover it from the existing claims: c011 and c041 concern antisymmetry and necessity, not whether undetermined reverse parthood is excluded. Nor does the revised r1 settle this, since it fixes which relation counts as proper parthood, not whether reverse parthood is determinate. The argument, as stated, does not survive this objection.

Revised premise: For God and each of God's parts, parthood is bivalent, so that God's being part of each such part is settled true rather than merely not false.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your three-valued catalogue exposes a genuine semantic gap if c008 is read with a weak, truth-value-gap-tolerant notion of “non-symmetric.” But that is not the relation the argument needs. On its intended reading, a part is proper exactly when its reverse parthood fails, and “God lacks proper parts” says: for every actual part x of God, it is not the case that God fails to be part of x. Given bivalence for this parthood relation, God must be part of every such x. That is the symmetry formulation, not an inference from mere epistemic non-confirmation. The paper itself presents viability as conditional on proper parthood being defined as non-symmetric [W7212186029.c011], and its similarity-relative account defines proper parthood with determinate structural features—irreflexivity, asymmetry, and transitivity [W7212186029.c018]. Your catalogue instead permits a third status precisely where the inference requires exclusion of it. So it is a countermodel to an unrestricted formulation of c008, but not to the strengthened, intended formulation. I concede that c008 as stated is under-specified: without determinacy or bivalence, the conclusion does not follow. This is a small repair, not a change in the theological thesis; it specifies the logic of the parthood relation used to formulate it. The resulting formulation remains distinct from identity where parthood is non-antisymmetric [W7212186029.c011].

Revised premise: For the similarity-relative parthood relation at issue, every parthood claim between God and one of God’s parts is determinate—true or false—and proper parthood is parthood whose reverse is false.

rounds.content: Your statues case is a real pressure point, but it targets a stronger claim than r1 makes. r1 says the similarity-relative relation tracks metaphysical constituency closely enough for the divine case, not that it tracks constituency in general. Your Ada and Ben pair shows that mutual similarity-parthood can hold between things with no shared constituents, and I accept that. What it does not show is that God's case is one of those unconstituted pairs. The relation is restricted, as c018 specifies, to properties and their bearers under the relevant similarity: God and omniscience are related as the instantiation model in c013 and r2 requires, where the parts are the divine properties themselves. Your own c016 says God and omniscience are mutual parts under similarity while remaining numerically distinct. You need a reason why, in the divine domain, the relation tracks constituency when it does not in the statue domain. Your rejoinder is right that the restriction to God's essential properties does not by itself supply constituency, and I should not pretend it does. The statues show that c018-parthood can hold between items with no constituency relation, as [W7212186029.c026] and the mutual-parts point make clear. But notice what the argument actually needs. It needs that having no proper parts under c018 is the traditional denial of composition. The denial of composition is a claim about God's having no metaphysical parts, and c016 and c013 treat the divine properties as parts only in a modelling sense, which is exactly the sense the traditional view must deny is constitutive. So the bridge fails unless the c018 relation is shown to track constituency where the traditional view says constituency is absent. The lack of proper parts without identity [W7212186029.c002] does not repair this, since it concerns the structure of the relation, not whether the relation carries metaphysical weight.

naive_questioner.question: If the whole point of divine simplicity is that God *doesn't* have proper parts, why does the conclusion say that God *is* a part of all God's parts—doesn't that mean God actually does have parts after all?

objection.text: Take a lamp, L, that is switched on at noon and off at one. Its property of being lit is instantiated at noon and not at one. Model instantiation as parthood: L is the fusion of its properties, so 'being lit' is a part of L. Now the lamp is switched off at one, and nothing in L's identity changes, yet the fusion has lost a part. But the fusion of its properties is supposed to be fixed by which properties it has, so the lamp at one o'clock is a different fusion from the lamp at noon, though it is the same lamp. Worse, the lamp also has the property of being a lamp, and that property is shared with every other lamp. A fusion of properties would then overlap with the fusion of a neighbouring lamp, so distinct objects share parts they should not share. Parthood cannot carry instantiation without either losing the lamp's persistence or making distinct objects overlap.
objection.premise_fails_because: c013 fails because treating instantiation as parthood over fusions of properties cannot preserve an object's identity through change in its properties while keeping distinct objects mereologically disjoint, since shared universals and temporary properties break the fusion model.

objection.text: Take a museum that holds two bronze casts, A and B, poured from one mold on the same day. They match atom-for-atom in shape, alloy and patina. On any similarity-based reading of parthood, each counts as part of the other, since everything A is like, B is like too. Yet a conservator melts A down and B stays on its plinth untouched. Nothing of B went into the crucible, so mutual similarity-parthood between distinct things is just duplication, not containment. Now apply this to God and omniscience. For the two to be similarity-parts of each other in both directions, omniscience would have to match God in every respect God has. But God knows that the casts exist, acts, and is omnipotent. Omniscience knows nothing, does nothing, and is not omnipotent. The resemblance holds only one way. Read narrowly, as similarity in the respect of knowing, the case collapses into the casts: mere matching between distinct items. Read broadly, it fails for lack of resemblance.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c016 fails because mutual similarity between numerically distinct items is mere duplication, as with the casts, and God and omniscience don't even match in every respect, so they cannot be genuine mutual parts while staying distinct.

objection.text: A believer describes God as wholly present in every act of understanding, loving, and creating, without treating these as separable components. When Mara prays for wisdom, she believes God knows her question, wills her good, and acts in one indivisible divine reality. She denies that knowledge, will, and action are proper parts of God: none can be detached, counted, or exist independently. Yet she also denies that divine simplicity is merely the absence of proper parts. For her, simplicity additionally means that God’s knowing, willing, and acting are identical with God, rather than distinct features somehow fused into a partless whole. A perfectly partless divine point containing three genuinely distinct, non-identical features would lack proper parts but would not satisfy her understanding of simplicity.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c006 fails because lacking proper parts does not by itself entail that God’s attributes are identical with God.

objection.text: A theologian maintains a three-valued parthood catalogue. It records omniscience as part of God, while whether God is part of omniscience is explicitly undetermined. A proper part is defined as a part whose reverse parthood is false, not merely unconfirmed. Omniscience is therefore not a proper part of God, and the catalogue contains no other candidate parts, so “God has no proper parts” is true. Yet “God is part of all God’s parts” is not true, because God’s parthood of omniscience remains undetermined. The absence of asymmetric parthood does not establish reciprocal parthood when undetermined relations are permitted. Premise W7212186029.c008 fails because having no proper parts does not yield symmetry when reverse parthood can be neither true nor false.

On Bo's model, God's omniscience is a proper part of God only if God is not identical to it, and God is part of omniscience only if omniscience includes God's whole nature. objection.text: Consider a chemist, Mara, studying a copper wire. She believes physical objects are composed of their physical constituents: atoms, fields, and their arrangements. She heats the wire, and it loses its coiled shape while every atom stays put. If the wire were a fusion of its properties, losing the property 'coiled' would mean losing a part. But nothing material left the wire. The wire also gains the property 'being thought of by Mara' when she reflects on it, yet no part arrives. They are not further ingredients. Treating instantiation as parthood confuses what an object is made of with what is true of it. The God case depends on this confusion: omniscience can be a 'part' of God only if parthood has been redefined until it no longer tracks composition. objection.text: skeptical theism: Mara believes God created a world whose deepest metaphysical structure exceeds human conceptual reach. She observes that a red apple instantiates redness and roundness, but she also believes God may ground these features through divine creative acts rather than by composing the apple from property-parts. When Mara tries to model instantiation as fusion, the model treats properties as separable constituents and assumes that creaturely mereology applies to every metaphysical dependence relation. turn.content:

But neither point establishes that any qualitative resemblance—for example, shared horse-shape across bronze and marble—constitutes a compositional relation. Your case therefore exposes a gap in r1, not merely an unwelcome consequence of the symmetry formulation. At most, the defender can say that the relevant resemblance is not property-sharing in the loose, shape-based sense; resemblance may instead concern sufficiently similar properties without a shared property [W7212186029.c034]. Yet that response by itself still does not connect resemblance to constituency. The argument survives only if its similarity relation is independently restricted to relations grounded in the divine attributes’ metaphysical constitution. Without that restriction, a thing could be materially composite while having no non-symmetric similarity-parts, exactly as you contend.

Revised premise: For God’s essential attributes, similarity-based parthood is restricted to resemblance relations grounded in metaphysical constituency, so merely qualitative similarity between independently constituted things never suffices for parthood.

objection.text: Consider two independently constituted things: a bronze statue, Ana, cast in Florence in 1500, and a bronze figurine, Ben, cast in Lyon in 1800, each with the same shape, mass, and surface colour. Nothing grounds their qualitative match in any shared constituent: they are made of distinct lumps of metal with no common part. Yet the revised premise says similarity grounded in metaphysical constituency is required for parthood, and that merely qualitative similarity between independently constituted things never suffices. Suppose a sculptor now proposes that Ana and Ben be treated as mutual parts with respect to shape, so that the fusion of their shapes is a single shape-bearer. The restriction blocks this only by fiat: it does not say what 'metaphysical constituency' contributes beyond the similarity itself, so the restriction is either idle or it smuggles in a constituency relation that the divine case, where God and God's attributes are not independently constituted, would need to supply by stipulation. Either way, the premise does not do the work the argument needs.
